The call came at four, while Nadia was sweeping brass filings off the floor of her aunt's shop. A man on Alder Street had locked himself out. Aunt Marisol took the small leather case from its hook, and Nadia, who had worked in the shop for three weeks and had so far been allowed to cut exactly one key, followed her out to the van.

The man was waiting on his front steps in his socks. He was perhaps seventy, with a folded newspaper under his arm, and he stood up too quickly when the van pulled in. "I stepped out for the paper," he said, "and the door swung shut behind me."

Aunt Marisol nodded and asked his name. Then she asked whether he had anything with this address on it, and whether a neighbor could say he lived here. Nadia felt her face go hot. The man was standing there in his socks. Anyone could see the house was his.

He patted his pockets and came up empty. Then he pointed across the street, and a woman watering her roses called out, "That's Mr. Duarte. He's lived there longer than I've lived here," and went back to her hose. Aunt Marisol wrote both names on her clipboard and handed Nadia the leather case.

"You do it," she said.

Nadia knelt at the lock. She had practiced on the clear plastic lock in the shop, where she could watch the five little pins rise and fall, but this one was solid brass and hid everything. She slid the tension wrench into the keyhole, pushed the pick in after it, and raked it hard across the pins, the way she had seen a thief do in a film. Nothing moved.

"Slower," her aunt said. "Find one pin. Lift it until you feel it set. Then the next."

It took Nadia eleven minutes. The third pin kept dropping back, and by the time she felt the cylinder turn, her knees ached from the concrete. Mr. Duarte thanked them both, twice, and went inside to find his wallet.

On the drive back, Nadia asked why her aunt had made such a fuss about the name and the neighbor. "He was obviously telling the truth."

"Probably," Aunt Marisol said. "I don't decide whether people are telling the truth. I check, the same way, every time. The day I start deciding by looking, I'm just a stranger who opens doors for whoever asks." She signaled at the corner. "The pins are the easy part. You'll have those by August."

Nadia looked down at the clipboard on her lap, at the two names in her aunt's square handwriting, and thought that August seemed a long way off for either part.

We built him in May from what the house
could spare: a broom handle, a feed sack
stuffed with straw, my grandfather's old work shirt
buttoned wrong, a pie tin for a face.

For a week the crows kept to the fence line.
They walked the top rail like inspectors
and looked at him from the side, one eye
and then the other, and did not come down.

By the second week one landed in the far row.
By the third, two of them were sitting
on his outstretched arms like a pair of cufflinks,
picking at the seed we had sown.

"They've learned him," my grandmother said,
the way she might have said it of a road
or a hymn. "Anything that stands in one place
long enough turns into a fence post."

That night, after supper, she went out
with a flashlight and pulled him up
and carried him, stiff as a ladder,
to the other end of the garden. She hung

a rattling string of bottle caps
from one sleeve and traded his hat
for the straw one from the porch,
and in the morning the crows stayed on the rail.

All summer it went on like that:
a new place every few days, a new sound,
a coat of white paint on the pie tin,
the shirt turned inside out, then back,

and every time, for a while, it worked,
and every time the crows came down again,
a little sooner, as if the lesson
were getting easier for them to learn.

I thought at first that the scarecrow
was what kept the garden. By August
I understood it was only the part
the crows could see, and that the rest of it

was out there every night with a flashlight,
pulling him up by the broom handle,
deciding where a stranger ought to stand.

The summer I was ten, my sister Tess came home from her first year of college able to juggle. She had learned it in a dormitory hallway from a boy who could keep five beanbags going while he talked, and she could manage three, which seemed to me the same as magic. I asked her to teach me before she had finished unpacking.

She handed me one beanbag. "Throw it from your right hand to your left," she said, "so it peaks just above your eyes. Then throw it back."

I threw it. I caught it. I looked at her for the next beanbag, and she shook her head. For the rest of that afternoon, and most of the next, I threw one beanbag back and forth across the porch while Tess read in the hammock and said "Higher" or "Too far forward" without looking up very often. I thought she was stalling. I suspected, privately, that she had forgotten how she learned and was inventing a method to keep me busy.

On the third day she gave me a second beanbag. Throw the first, she said, and when it peaks, throw the second underneath it. Then stop. Let them both fall if you have to. I let them both fall for a long time. The point, she kept telling me, was the throws. "The catches take care of themselves if the throws are right. Every bad catch you make is a bad throw you made a second earlier."

I did not believe this. It sounded like something printed on a poster in a gym. But I started watching my throws instead of my hands, and the beanbags began landing where my hands already were.

It took me most of July to keep three going for a count of twenty. Tess was packing for school again by then. She watched from the doorway with a sweater half folded and said, "There," and went back to packing.

I have taught perhaps a dozen people to juggle since then, and every one of them has looked at me, when I handed over a single beanbag, with the expression I must have given Tess on the porch. I have tried, each time, to explain why we start with one. It has never worked. The explanation only makes sense once you have spent two days throwing one beanbag, and by then you have stopped needing it.

She had learned it in a dormitory hallway from a boy who could keep five beanbags going while he talked, and she could manage three, which seemed to me the same as magic. I asked her to teach me before she had finished unpacking.

She handed me one beanbag. "Throw it from your right hand to your left," she said, "so it peaks just above your eyes. Then throw it back."

I threw it. I caught it. I looked at her for the next beanbag, and she shook her head. For the rest of that afternoon, and most of the next, I threw one beanbag back and forth across the porch while Tess read in the hammock and said "Higher" or "Too far forward" without looking up very often. I thought she was stalling. I suspected, privately, that she had forgotten how she learned and was inventing a method to keep me busy.

On the third day she gave me a second beanbag. Throw the first, she said, and when it peaks, throw the second underneath it. Then stop. Let them both fall if you have to. I let them both fall for a long time. The point, she kept telling me, was the throws. "The catches take care of themselves if the throws are right. Every bad catch you make is a bad throw you made a second earlier."

I did not believe this. It sounded like something printed on a poster in a gym. But I started watching my throws instead of my hands, and the beanbags began landing where my hands already were.

It took me most of July to keep three going for a count of twenty. Tess was packing for school again by then. She watched from the doorway with a sweater half folded and said, "There," and went back to packing.

I have taught perhaps a dozen people to juggle since then, and every one of them has looked at me, when I handed over a single beanbag, with the expression I must have given Tess on the porch. I have tried, each time, to explain why we start with one. It has never worked. The explanation only makes sense once you have spent two days throwing one beanbag, and by then you have stopped needing it.

The first newspaper in Calder Ferry was printed in the back room of a harness shop in the spring of 1868. Its editor, Amos Wetherell, had bought a secondhand press from a paper that had failed two counties away and hauled it home in pieces on a farm wagon. The first issue of the Calder Ferry Courier ran to four pages. Most of the front page was copied, with credit, from the newspapers of larger cities, which reached the town by mail a week or two after they were printed. The local news filled half a column on the back.

Wetherell meant the Courier to be a window on the wider world. He printed long reports of debates in the state legislature, letters from travelers abroad, and the prices of grain in markets three hundred miles away. By the end of the first summer he had sixty-one subscribers, and a good number of them paid in cordwood, eggs or flour, since cash was scarce along the river. The press, he wrote to his brother, was costing him more than it earned.

The change began with a horse. In August a farmer named Silas Dunn walked into the harness shop with twenty-five cents and asked Wetherell to print three lines about a bay mare with one white foreleg that had broken through his fence. The notice ran on the back page. Eight days later a family from the far side of Mill Creek, eleven miles off, led the mare into town. They had been about to light their kitchen stove with that week's Courier and had read the notice before striking the match.

The next week four people brought notices: a lost pocketbook, a plow found in a ditch, a church supper, a school in need of a teacher. Within a year the Courier was running two full columns of them under the heading "Of Local Interest." In the spring of 1869 Wetherell moved the column to the front page and the legislature to the third. Subscriptions passed three hundred that winter.

It was, in its small way, the most useful thing the Courier ever printed. Families in the outlying districts, who came to town perhaps once a month, could now learn of an auction before it was over. The county commissioners began sending their minutes to be printed. A woman who had lived in Calder Ferry since before the war later recalled that, until the Courier, news had traveled by whoever happened to stop at the mill.

Wetherell edited the paper for nearly thirty years. In a column marking its twenty-fifth year, he wrote that he had come to Calder Ferry intending to bring the world to the town, and had spent his life showing the town to itself.

A young Pacific salmon spends its first weeks or months, and in some species a year or more, in the fresh water where it hatched. Then it swims downstream to the ocean, where it may travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometers as it feeds and grows. After one to several years, depending on the species, it turns back.
